ann_34.original: Three nodes in series. Node 148 is on for every training patient (share 100% of 242) and rises with the number of major vessels coloured (ca): in the typical case it is 0.40 at 0 vessels and 1.01 at 3 vessels; through its edge to the output (weight 1.66) it is a second, smaller ca term next to the direct one, and it also feeds node 2034. Node 7566 is on for exactly the training patients with a normal thallium scan: the rows where its on-state and the scan disagree number 0. Node 2034 is an age brake for patients with normal fasting blood sugar, and it lowers the score when on. It is on for 82 training patients, only 4 of them under 55, and it is never on for the 33 training patients with high fasting sugar (0 of them have it on). Self-probe (whole model, typical case with a reversible defect): with normal fasting sugar the node first opens at 60 years among the probed ages (value 0.25); predicted risk is highest at 55 years (65%) and then falls to 31% at 75 years as the node grows (value 1.80); with high fasting sugar the node stays at 0.00 and risk keeps rising, to 47% at 75 years. A normal scan (node 7566 on) holds the brake back: at 60 years node 2034 is 0.00 with a normal scan and 0.25 with a reversible defect. With a fixed defect the node is open across the probed ages and pushes predicted risk down hard: in the typical case risk is 8% at 40 years and 1% at 70 years, against 43% and 42% for a reversible defect at the same ages. That regime is fitted to the 15 training patients with a fixed defect (10 of them have the node on); their mean predicted risk is still 56%, because an abnormal scan also opens the oldpeak gate, which pushes the other way. Switching the whole part off lowers training AUC from the full model's 0.9605 to 0.9460. In short, from about 60 years the model stops adding risk for age, and then lowers it, in patients with normal fasting sugar; and it offsets the abnormal-scan boost for patients with a fixed defect.

ann_35.original: Adds predicted risk as ST depression on exercise (oldpeak) rises, with a threshold set by the thallium scan. For patients whose scan is not normal the gate opens at almost no ST depression: in the typical case with a reversible defect its node value is 0.10 at 0 mm, and the whole-model predicted risk rises from 29% there to 77% at 1 mm. With a normal scan it stays shut much longer: risk is 26% at 1 mm, the node is still 0.001 at 2 mm, and risk climbs only beyond that (74% at 3 mm). Typical angina also closes it: in the whole model, a typical patient with a reversible defect and 1 mm of ST depression has predicted risk 9% with typical angina against 77% with no chest pain (node value 0.00 against 1.31). On the training data it is on for 99 of the 107 patients whose scan is not normal but for 11 of the 135 with a normal scan; over the 110 patients it acts on, it adds 3.11 to the score (logit) on average. Switching it off lowers training AUC from the full model's 0.9605 to 0.9187. In short, the model reads ST depression as a strong warning mainly when the thallium scan is abnormal.
ann_35.proposed: Adds risk as ST depression on exercise rises past about 2.0 mm, more steeply with an abnormal thallium scan (for a typical patient from about 29% to about 99% against about 26% to about 65% with a normal scan); for the 22 training patients with typical angina it does not change the risk up to 2.8 mm. It acts on 110 of 242 training patients.

ann_36.original: Cancels the blood-pressure slope for patients without exercise-induced angina. Resting blood pressure has a direct term of 0.84 per sd on the score through its own edge; this gate also rises with blood pressure (and with absence of exercise angina, and with female sex) and enters the output with a negative weight, so when it is open it takes back about as much as the direct term adds. On the training data it is open for 156 of the 160 patients with no exercise angina, but for 5 of the 82 with exercise angina (that regime is fitted to 5 rows). Self-probe (whole model, typical case): with no exercise angina the predicted risk is 26% at 120 mm Hg and 24% at 180 mm Hg, so blood pressure barely moves it; with exercise angina, where the gate stays closed (node value 0.00 even at 180 mm Hg), risk rises from 21% to 81% over the same range. At 100 mm Hg the gate is closed even without exercise angina (node value 0.00). Female sex lowers its threshold: for a typical patient with exercise angina at 180 mm Hg the node is 1.40 for a woman and 0.00 for a man. Over the 161 training patients it acts on, its mean contribution to the score (logit) is -1.80. Switching it off lowers training AUC from the full model's 0.9605 to 0.9409. In short, the model treats high blood pressure as a risk factor for patients who get angina on exercise, and largely ignores it for those who do not.
ann_36.proposed: Lowers the risk as blood pressure rises for patients without chest pain on exercise, so that in the whole model higher blood pressure raises the predicted risk for patients with chest pain on exercise (for a typical patient from about 14% to about 57%) and barely moves it for the others. It acts on 161 of 242 training patients, nearly all without chest pain on exercise, and lowers the risk further for women.

ann_37.original: The linear part of the score: the inputs that reach the output through their own edges. Weights are per sd of the z-scored input, measured along each edge. The largest are the number of major vessels coloured, ca (1.33), a flat ST slope (1.08), resting blood pressure (0.84), male sex (0.71), high fasting blood sugar (-0.68), cholesterol (0.62), non-anginal chest pain (-0.59) and age (0.56); the rest are smaller. Self-probes (whole model, typical case): for ST slope the predicted risk is 26% with an upsloping segment, 69% with a flat one and 16% with a downsloping one, so the model treats a flat slope, not a downsloping one, as the warning sign. Risk rises steeply with vessels coloured, from 26% at 0 vessels to 99% at 3 vessels, with this part's output going from -0.11 to 4.37 (node 148 adds a little more). High fasting blood sugar lowers the predicted risk in the typical case, from 26% to 5%; the age brake in the thal_ca_age_gate part reverses that gap in older patients (with a reversible defect at 75 years, risk is 31% with normal and 47% with high fasting sugar). Switching the whole part to its mean lowers training AUC from the full model's 0.9605 to 0.8402, the largest loss of any part.
ann_37.proposed: A weighted sum: more vessels, a flat ST segment, higher blood pressure, higher cholesterol and older age each raise the predicted risk steadily (for a typical patient, vessels from about 26% to about 87%, blood pressure from about 12% to about 52%); high fasting blood sugar, non-anginal chest pain, being a woman and chest pain on exercise each lower it.

ann_38.original: The predicted risk is a sigmoid of a sum on the logit scale: the direct terms, plus the oldpeak gate and node 148 (which add risk), plus the sex/blood-pressure/exercise-angina gate and the age brake, node 2034 (which subtract it). The children combine additively at the output; the serial chain (nodes 148 and 7566 feeding node 2034) sits inside the thal_ca_age_gate part. By ablation, the direct terms matter most (training AUC from the full model's 0.9605 to 0.8402 without them), then the oldpeak gate (0.9187), the blood-pressure gate (0.9409) and the thal/ca/age part (0.9460). Self-probe (whole model, typical case with 2 mm of ST depression): an abnormal scan and diseased vessels each push risk up and together saturate it; predicted risk is 26% with a normal scan and 0 vessels, 93% with a normal scan and 2 vessels, 97% with a reversible defect and 0 vessels, and above 99% with both. The model's main story: vessels coloured and a flat ST slope add risk linearly; ST depression adds risk mainly when the thallium scan is abnormal; blood pressure counts mainly for patients with exercise angina; and from about 60 years, age stops adding risk for patients with normal fasting sugar.
ann_38.proposed: The model adds up four parts. For a typical patient (predicted risk about 26%), more vessels coloured raise the predicted risk steadily to about 93% at 2 vessels, a flat ST segment to about 69% and more ST depression to about 65%; being a woman lowers it to about 1% and high fasting blood sugar to about 5%. Blood pressure counts for patients with chest pain on exercise, and ST depression when the chest pain is not typical angina.

lead.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, a normal thallium scan, no vessels coloured and median test results), the model predicts a risk of heart disease of about 26%.

It builds that prediction by adding up four parts: a sum of inputs that each add or remove a fixed amount, a switch for ST depression on exercise, a part that ties resting blood pressure to chest pain on exercise, and a part that adjusts for vessels, age, fasting blood sugar and the thallium scan.

ann_34.text: A higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if age is at or below 56 years (steadily, each extra vessel adding about the same for patients with age at or below 56 years): for a typical patient, number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy going from 0 vessels to 2 vessels moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 17% to about 89% if age is at or below 56 years, and from about 33% to about 92% if age is above 56 years.

For a typical patient, age going from 42 years to 66 years moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 7% to about 1% if the thallium scan shows a fixed defect, and from about 13% to about 27% if the thallium scan is normal (it moves steadily for most patients, but for some patients with fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL (5 of the 5 sampled) it peaks inside the range for patients with a fixed defect on the thallium scan). The model has little data on this: only 15 training patients (a fixed defect on the thallium scan).

For a typical patient, age going from 42 years to 66 years moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 2% to about 8% if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL, and from about 13% to about 27% if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less (it moves steadily for most patients, but for some patients with a fixed defect on the thallium scan (5 of the 5 sampled) it peaks inside the range for patients with fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL).

The model gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease if the thallium scan shows a fixed defect than if the thallium scan is normal, and even more so if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less: for a typical patient, going from a normal thallium scan to a fixed defect on the thallium scan moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 26% to about 2% if fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less, and from about 5% to about 22% if fasting blood sugar is above 120 mg/dL. The model has little data on this: only 15 training patients (a fixed defect on the thallium scan).

Other effects: a fixed defect on the thallium scan (rather than a normal thallium scan) lowers it; thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded) (rather than a normal thallium scan) raises it; a higher number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy raises it in an uneven way; age past about 61 years lowers it with nothing until about 61 years (between 56 and 62 years for different patients), then steadily; a higher age lowers it with nothing until about 61 years (between 56 and 62 years for different patients), then steadily (on the training data only). The model has little data on some of these: only 15 training patients (a fixed defect on the thallium scan) and 2 training patients (thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded)).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL (rather than fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less) raises it; a reversible defect on the thallium scan (rather than a normal thallium scan) lowers it (on the training data only).

ann_35.text: This part acts on 110 of 242 training patients (45%).
For a typical patient it acts on, it clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 94% without this part to above 99% with it.
In the training data, 81 of these 110 patients had heart disease.

The model gives a clearly higher predicted risk of heart disease if thallium stress test result is something other than a normal thallium scan than if the thallium scan is normal, mainly if chest pain type is something other than typical angina (it also changes for 11 of the 22 training patients for whom it does not hold): for a typical patient, going from a normal thallium scan to thallium stress test result other than a normal thallium scan moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 26% to about 67% if chest pain type is something other than typical angina, and from about 9% to about 9% if the patient has typical angina.

A higher ST depression on exercise clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, but only if chest pain type is something other than typical angina (in an uneven way for patients with chest pain type other than typical angina): for a typical patient, ST depression on exercise going from 0.0 mm to 2.8 mm moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 26% to about 65% if chest pain type is something other than typical angina, and from about 9% to about 9% if the patient has typical angina (above 2.8 mm it changes for them too: from about 9% to about 63% at 6.2 mm).

ann_36.text: This part acts on 161 of 242 training patients (67%); nearly all of them are patients without chest pain on exercise.
